topic.en: Three sections: a station lost property office and a walks programme, a first week in IT and overtime rules, and an essay on why birds sing before dawn.

textTitles: Your first week: IT accounts and equipment
Overtime: how it is agreed and paid

paragraphs.text: Central Station lost property office. Items found on trains arriving at Central Station and anywhere in the station building are brought to the lost property office on platform 1. The office is open from 8 am to 6 pm on weekdays and from 9 am to 1 pm on Saturdays; it is closed on Sundays and public holidays. Items found at other stations on the line are kept at those stations for one week before being sent here.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: To reclaim an item, report the loss online or at the office, describing the item and the train or place where you think you left it. When we find a match we will contact you by email. You will need to bring photo identification and pay a handling charge of £3 for each item; there is no charge for children’s items or for travel passes, which are returned to the issuing office.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: We keep items for four weeks, after which they are given to charity or, in the case of electronic goods, securely destroyed. Food, drinks and perishable items are thrown away at the end of the day on which they are found. We cannot post items to you, but someone else may collect on your behalf if they bring a signed letter from you and their own identification.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Castle Hill and the Old Town (Saturday, 10 am, 2 hours). An easy walk through the historic centre, finishing at the castle gate, where the guide explains how the town grew up around the river crossing. The route is on pavements throughout and is suitable for wheelchairs and pushchairs. £6, children free.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Wetland Birds (Saturday, 7.30 am, 3 hours). An early start to see wading birds feeding at low tide. The paths are flat but can be muddy, so waterproof boots are essential. Binoculars can be borrowed from the visitor centre for a deposit of £10. £8; not suitable for children under 10.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Ridge and Reservoir (Sunday, 9 am, 5 hours). Our longest and most demanding walk, with two steep climbs and wide views across the valley. Bring a packed lunch, as there are no shops on the route. Walkers should be confident on rough ground and able to keep a steady pace. £8; dogs on leads are welcome.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Gardens of the Riverside Houses (Sunday, 2 pm, 90 minutes). A gentle walk visiting four private gardens that are opened specially for the tour, with tea and cake at the last one included in the price. Numbers are limited to fifteen, so booking is essential. £12; no dogs, as the gardens are private.
paragraphs.label: D

texts.label: C
texts.title: Your first week: IT accounts and equipment

paragraphs.text: Your first week: IT accounts and equipment. Your user account is created before you start, and your line manager will give you a temporary password on your first morning. You must change it the first time you log in; the new password must be at least twelve characters long and must not include your name or the name of the company. You will also be asked to set up two-step verification using the authenticator app on your work phone, and you cannot access email until this has been done.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Laptops and phones are issued by the IT service desk on the ground floor, which is open from 8.30 am to 5 pm. Bring your staff pass, as the desk cannot release equipment without it. You will be asked to sign an equipment form confirming what you have received; keep a copy, because the same form is used to check equipment when you leave the company. Headsets, keyboards and monitors for home working can be ordered through the online catalogue and are delivered within five working days.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Company equipment is for work use, although reasonable personal use of email and the internet during breaks is allowed. Do not install software yourself: request it through the service desk, which checks that it is licensed and safe. Files should be saved to the shared drive rather than to the laptop itself, because the shared drive is backed up every night and the laptop is not.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: If a device is lost or stolen, report it to the service desk immediately, day or night, using the emergency number on the back of your staff pass; the device can then be locked and its data erased remotely. If you suspect that an email is a phishing attempt, do not click any links, and forward it to the security team using the button in your email program. Nobody from IT will ever ask you for your password.
paragraphs.label: D

texts.label: D
texts.title: Overtime: how it is agreed and paid

paragraphs.text: Overtime: how it is agreed and paid. Overtime is any work beyond your contracted hours that your manager has asked for or approved in advance. Work done without approval is not paid, however long it takes, so if you think a task cannot be finished in your normal hours, speak to your manager before you stay late rather than afterwards. Travel time to a job outside your usual workplace counts as working time. Part-time staff who work extra hours are paid at their normal rate until they reach the full-time working week, and at overtime rates only after that.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Overtime is paid at one and a half times your normal hourly rate on weekdays and Saturdays, and at double your normal rate on Sundays and public holidays. As an alternative to payment, you may choose to take time off in lieu, calculated hour for hour rather than at the enhanced rate. Time off in lieu must be taken within three months, or it will be lost; it cannot be carried over into the following year.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Record overtime on your timesheet in the week it is worked, with a brief note of the task. Your manager approves the timesheet, and overtime approved by the 20th of the month is paid with that month’s salary; anything approved later is paid the following month. Missing or late timesheets are the most common reason for delayed payment. If you believe an overtime payment is wrong, raise it with payroll within two months of the payment date.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: No employee is required to work more than an average of 48 hours a week, including overtime, unless they have signed an agreement to do so, and such an agreement can be cancelled with seven days’ notice. Managers are asked to share overtime fairly and to avoid relying on the same people week after week. Staff who feel they are being asked to work too much overtime should speak to their manager or to human resources.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Anyone who has woken early in spring knows the sound: in the hour before sunrise, the birds of a garden or wood begin to sing together, rising to a peak shortly before the sun appears and falling away as the morning goes on. The dawn chorus is one of the most familiar events in nature and, surprisingly, one of the least understood. Several explanations have been proposed over the past century, and researchers now suspect that no single one of them is sufficient, which is part of what makes the subject interesting. It happens, after all, in almost every garden.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The first thing to understand is who is singing and why. In most temperate species it is the males that sing, and song serves two main purposes: it announces to rival males that a territory is occupied and defended, and it attracts females. Both functions are most important in spring, when territories are being established and pairs are forming, which is why the chorus is loudest in the breeding season and much quieter, or absent, for the rest of the year. In a few species females sing as well, and in the tropics duets between partners are common, which suggests that the northern pattern is not the only one.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: One long-standing explanation concerns sound itself. In the early morning the air is often still and cool, and it has been claimed that song travels further at dawn than at any other time, so that a bird singing then advertises itself over a wider area. Measurements have given mixed support to this idea. Sound does carry well on calm mornings, but the advantage over late morning is small in many habitats, and it does not explain why birds that sing at dawn often remain quiet on equally calm evenings. The idea remains popular in field guides, but most researchers now treat it as a minor factor at best.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: A second explanation looks at what else a bird could be doing. At first light it is too dark for many species to find insects efficiently, so the time is of little value for feeding, and a bird loses less by singing then than it would later in the day. On this view the chorus is not a sign that dawn is especially good for singing, but that it is especially poor for everything else. Supporters point out that species with larger eyes, which can forage in dimmer light, tend to begin singing later than those with small eyes. The pattern is not perfect, but it has been found in several separate studies.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: A third idea concerns energy. A small bird loses a great deal of its body weight overnight simply keeping warm, and it cannot be certain in the evening how much it will have left by morning. If it survives the night with reserves to spare, singing strongly at dawn is a way of spending the surplus, and perhaps of showing rivals and females that it is in good condition. Experiments in which some birds were given extra food in the evening found that they sang more the next morning, which fits this explanation, although not all studies have produced the same result.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Social factors are also involved. Females of many species are most fertile in the early morning, and a male that sings then may be guarding his mate, reminding rivals that he is present at the time they are most likely to intrude. In some species the males that begin singing earliest also have more offspring, which suggests that an early start is itself attractive. Because each male responds to his neighbours, the chorus may also build on itself: once a few birds start, others join to avoid being outsung. In dense populations, a chorus can therefore become louder than any individual bird needs it to be.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Artificial light has complicated the picture in towns and cities. Studies have found that birds living near street lights begin singing earlier than those in dark areas, sometimes long before the first natural light, and in some places they sing at night. Noise may play a part as well: birds in cities with heavy morning traffic start earlier, apparently to finish before the loudest period of the day. The long-term effects on the health and breeding of these birds are not yet known, but researchers regard urban choruses as a useful natural experiment. Some species appear to have adapted by shifting the pitch of their songs upwards, above the low hum of traffic.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: What emerges from this research is not one answer but several, each partly true and each more important for some species than for others. The dawn chorus is best understood as the combined result of physical conditions, the timing of feeding, the state of each bird’s reserves and the pressures of competition and courtship. For the listener, none of this makes the sound less remarkable. If anything, knowing how many different needs are being met at once makes the early hours of a spring morning more interesting than any single explanation could. The chorus, in other words, is a crowd of different reasons singing together.
paragraphs.label: H
